newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish pharmas challenge state on reimbursement.
newsitem.headline: Finnish pharmas challenge state on reimbursement.

text.p: The Finnish Pharmaceutical Industry Federation said on Thursday it had appealed to the European Commission to force Finland to tighten up its procedure on giving patients back some of the cost of special drugs.

In a statement charging the Republic of Finland with "negligence", the federation said the current system by which patients can receive extra money back on new, more efficient drugs is too slow and breaks European Union rules.
"The procedure of the Finnish state is both contrary to law and also questionable from a human perspective," it said: as well as being slow the system was "parsimonious".

Basic Finnish medical care entitles patients to reclaim 50 percent of the cost of drugs after a 50 markka ($9.73) charge; on some medicines the repayment can rise to 75 percent or 100 percent, after a 25 markka payment.

The federation's lawyer, Olli-Pekka Myllynen, said drugs being held back by delays in the system included new treatments for Alzheimer's disease. Approval for reimbursement on one treatment had been tied up in the system for two years, he said.
"People know they are available but they cannot have them -- most of them are higher-priced and the average retired person can't pay the expense of those," he said by telephone.

The federation, which has over 50 members including many overseas pharmaceuticals companies, believed the delays combined with a lack of transparency in the system could also in effect be limiting imports of drugs to Finland, he said.
The federation said in its statement that it had failed to resolve the dispute with Finland's social affairs and health ministry, which was why it was taking the issue to the European Commission.
No one at the ministry was available to comment. The Finnish government has been gradually trimming its spending on reimbursements of medical costs as part of a cost-cutting programme.
